article_html:
• ISPR DG warns Taliban against testing Pakistan.
  • Says Kabul regime harbouring terrorist leaders.
  • Says military adapting to changing warfare technologies.

RAWALPINDI: The Afghan Taliban do not have the capability to absorb the “punishment” Pakistan can inflict in response to threats emanating from Afghanistan, the military’s spokesperson has warned.

Director General Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry told Reuters Pakistan possessed the capability to counter threats from the Afghan Taliban, including those involving drones, and was prepared for attempts to test its operational readiness.

“Whatever they want to send, they can; they may try. We have the capability to take them on,” the ISPR DG said in an interview.

“They don’t have, I think, the capability to then absorb the punishment that we can put on them,” he added.

The military spokesperson was responding to a question about the potential threat posed by drones in the hands of the Afghan Taliban and whether Pakistan could face a situation similar to drone threats elsewhere in the region.

Lt Gen Chaudhry said that whatever drone capability the Afghan Taliban possessed was not indigenous, saying that such technology was being supplied by their sponsors.

The ISPR DG said that India is the “biggest terror sponsor” in the context of threats facing Pakistan and added that the Afghan Taliban and terrorist groups operating against Pakistan were acting as Indian proxies.

Referring to Pakistan’s previous conflict with India, he said New Delhi had sent “dozens and dozens” of sophisticated drones, which Pakistan successfully countered.

“We turned them into dust everywhere,” he said, adding that Pakistan had since moved further ahead in terms of its operational readiness.

'There will be a cost'

The ISPR DG also said that the Afghan Taliban regime is harbouring terrorist leaders and allowing armed groups to operate from Afghan soil against Pakistan.

He said Islamabad was not seeking Afghanistan’s isolation and remained engaged with Kabul, but expected the Afghan Taliban to “act like a state” and prevent terrorism from its territory.

“We only ask you that don’t support terrorism inside Pakistan. Stop harbouring the terrorist leaders,” he said.

The spokesperson said that terrorist formations were coming from Afghanistan and receiving weapons from there, while Afghan citizens and even personnel of the Taliban regime had been found among groups involved in attacks against Pakistan.

“If you do it, then there will be a cost,” he warned. “And we are capable of imposing that cost and we have a clear strategy how to impose that cost.”

He also said that Afghanistan are providing an environment where multiple militant organisations were able to operate, while rejecting allegations that Pakistan was hosting or coordinating anti-Taliban elements.

'Afghanistan producing terrorism and drugs'

Rejecting the suggestion that Kabul should be isolated, the ISPR DG said the international community and regional countries instead needed to engage the Afghan Taliban and press them to behave like a state.

“What Afghanistan is producing right now, it has only two products: terrorism and drugs,” he said, adding that both posed threats to the region and the wider world.

The spokesperson said Pakistan had no interest in dictating how Afghanistan should be governed, maintaining that this was for Afghans to decide.

He stressed, however, that armed groups, militias and mercenaries could not be tolerated by any state.

Pakistan Army 'technology-savvy'

Discussing the changing nature of warfare, the ISPR DG said the Pakistan Army was adapting its capabilities to emerging threats across conventional and non-contact warfare, including drones and cyber technologies.

He said the proliferation of non-contact warfare capabilities among non-state actors posed a threat that required countries to reassess their security architecture.

Asked whether the military used artificial intelligence to identify targets in Afghanistan, the spokesperson declined to disclose operational details.

“I cannot go into specifics [about] how we are using AI, how we are using quantum technology, how we are using cyber technology, or how we are using multiple other technologies,” he said.

“But we are using all sorts of technologies. We are a technology-savvy army.”

headline: World Bank approves $150m programme to improve municipal services in Sindh
subheadline: Initiative will benefit 25 local councils in Karachi, serving a population of 3.58 million, says lender
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Programme targets improved property tax collection.
Karachi's annual property tax target rises to $85m.
70% of property tax revenue to fund local services.

The World Bank has approved $150 million in financing for a programme aimed at improving urban property tax collection and strengthening municipal service delivery in Sindh.

The World Bank Group's Board of Executive Directors approved the financing for the Sindh Property Revenues Enhancement Program (Sindh PREP) on October 30, a statement read.

"Cities that can raise their own revenues can plan and invest for the long term," said Bolormaa Amgaabazar, World Bank Country Director for Pakistan.

"Today, Sindh's local councils depend on provincial transfers for more than 95% of their revenues. By helping Karachi collect the property taxes from its residents and businesses, and by reinvesting most of that revenue in local services, this programme will give Sindh's cities the means to finance the infrastructure they need," she added.

The Sindh PREP will support the provincial government in improving urban immovable property tax (UIPT) collection and strengthening municipal service delivery capacity in selected local councils.

Despite being one of the world's largest cities, Karachi currently collects only around $8.5 million annually in property tax, while cities of similar size collect between 82 and 350 times more.

The programme aims to increase Karachi's annual property tax collection to $85 million and raise compliance from 20% to 50%.

It will achieve this by strengthening property tax collection, compliance and administration, including through the introduction of a UIPT management information system for billing, payment processing and grievance redress. Integrated financial management information systems will also be rolled out across local councils.

Around 70% of the collected property tax revenue will be reinvested directly into municipal infrastructure and services in participating local councils.

The programme will benefit Karachi's 25 local councils, with 3.58 million people living in these areas identified as its primary beneficiaries.

Funding will be linked to results, with annual performance assessments conducted by an Independent Verification Agent determining the awards each council receives.

These awards will finance the rehabilitation of climate-resilient municipal infrastructure and services, including drainage, sewerage, schools, fire stations, roads and street lighting.

The programme also includes a $40 million Investment Project Financing component to expand property surveys and property tax administration to 20 local councils in other urban centres of Sindh.

Around 4.5 million people in these areas are expected to benefit indirectly.

By helping Karachi collect the property taxes from its residents and businesses, and by reinvesting most of that revenue in local services, this programme will give Sindh's cities the means to finance the infrastructure they need," she added.
The Sindh PREP will support the provincial government in improving urban immovable property tax (UIPT) collection and strengthening municipal service delivery capacity in selected local councils.
Despite being one of the world's largest cities, Karachi currently collects only around $8.5 million annually in property tax, while cities of similar size collect between 82 and 350 times more.
The programme aims to increase Karachi's annual property tax collection to $85 million and raise compliance from 20% to 50%.

It will achieve this by strengthening property tax collection, compliance and administration, including through the introduction of a UIPT management information system for billing, payment processing and grievance redress. Integrated financial management information systems will also be rolled out across local councils.
Around 70% of the collected property tax revenue will be reinvested directly into municipal infrastructure and services in participating local councils.
The programme will benefit Karachi's 25 local councils, with 3.58 million people living in these areas identified as its primary beneficiaries.
Funding will be linked to results, with annual performance assessments conducted by an Independent Verification Agent determining the awards each council receives.
These awards will finance the rehabilitation of climate-resilient municipal infrastructure and services, including drainage, sewerage, schools, fire stations, roads and street lighting.
The programme also includes a $40 million Investment Project Financing component to expand property surveys and property tax administration to 20 local councils in other urban centres of Sindh.
Around 4.5 million people in these areas are expected to benefit indirectly.

headline: Princess Anne makes rare remark about power of connection in London
subheadline: Princess Anne shares thoughtful words on one thing she believes brings people closer together
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Princess Anne has shared her thoughts on the power of bringing people together during a creative evening in London.

The Princess Royal attended the 2026 Patron’s Lecture at the Royal Society of Arts (RSA) on 2 October, where she praised the organisation’s fellowship and the value of exchanging ideas.

Speaking about the community, Anne described the RSA Fellowship as “a truly extraordinary resource”, adding: “I think people do this better when they meet together.”

Read More: Princess Anne takes on £15m royal opening celebrating Britain's elite commandos

As Patron of the RSA, Princess Anne joined an event focused on creativity, education and the role of collaboration in turning new ideas into reality.

The lecture was delivered by writer and activist Scarlett Curtis, who explored how creative thinking can move beyond imagination and find its place in everyday life.

Following the lecture, Scarlett joined Deborah Meaden, Liv Little and Richard Curtis for a panel discussion on creativity, arts education and the importance of giving people the freedom to experiment.

The evening also saw the launch of a new RSA pocketbook, How Ideas Get Made, which looks at the conditions that allow different minds to flourish and creative ideas to take shape.

headline: LPG 'crisis' grips Pakistan ahead of winter; prices climb as high as Rs700 per kg
subheadline: Supply disruption at Taftan border triggers shortage as official price rises
author: Web Desk
article_text:
LPG unavailable at official Rs294 per kg.
Prices reach Rs700 per kg in Balochistan.
Petroleum minister assures ample gas supply in winter.

Pakistan is facing a severe liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) shortage ahead of winter as supplies through the Taftan border remain suspended, pushing retail prices to as high as Rs700 per kilogramme in parts of the country, Geo News reported on Sunday.

The shortage comes as the official LPG price has also been increased by Rs14 per kg to Rs294 per kg, according to a notification. However, consumers said the commodity was not available at the government-notified rate.

In Quetta and other parts of Balochistan, LPG was being sold for between Rs530 and Rs700 per kg, while prices in Karachi and Lahore ranged from Rs520 to Rs580 per kg.

In Peshawar, the commodity was selling for between Rs600 and Rs650 per kg.

Consumers in Lahore, meanwhile, said LPG was being sold at shops for Rs550 to Rs600 per kg despite the official price of Rs294, calling on the government to bring prices down.

Hormuz situation affecting oil, gas prices

Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik, speaking at a private university’s convocation in Lahore, said uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz had affected oil and gas prices.

He said Pakistan had successfully navigated the situation over the past six months and maintained that petroleum prices were determined through a transparent mechanism.

Malik said gas supplies were arriving from Qatar and assured that ample supplies would continue during December and January.

He also said the government was providing subsidised petrol to low-income people.

LPG marketers raise concerns over proposed policy

Meanwhile, Pakistan LPG Marketers Association Senior Vice President Ali Haider said a summary concerning the LPG pricing policy had been sent to the prime minister.

Haider said the proposed policy would make LPG 25% to 30% more expensive and maintained that it had been formulated without consultation with stakeholders.

He said higher LPG prices would hurt both businesses and consumers and called on the government to deregulate the sector.

headline: Michael Douglas reveals what Jack Nicholson is up to after leaving Hollywood
subheadline: Jack Nicholson, 89, made his final on-screen appearance in 2010's 'How Do You Know'
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Jack Nicholson is enjoying his well-deserved retirement, according to his close pal Michael Douglas.

While promoting his new memoir, One Helluva Ride, at a recent event in Swansea, Wales, Douglas admitted he “would have liked to have acted with” Nicholson, per The Independent.

But, Douglas noted, “He’s not working any more. He’s well. He has disappeared. I know that.”

READ MORE: Jack Nicholson shares unfiltered thoughts on his celebrity status

Although the two never starred in a film together, Douglas produced the 1975 drama One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest, which featured Nicholson in his Oscar-winning role.

“I still see him, but he is fine,” Douglas, 82, continued. “He is up there by his house and walking around in his slippers. It happens. He deserves it. I understand. He is a few years older than me, but I understand.”

Nicholson, 89, has not appeared in a film since 2010’s How Do You Know, though he has never formally announced his retirement. His last public appearance was in February 2025 at the Saturday Night Live 50th anniversary special.

His daughter, Lorraine, offered fans a rare glimpse of the actor on his 89th birthday in April, sharing a photo of him spending time with singer Joni Mitchell.

READ MORE: Jack Nicholson's daughter Lorraine celebrates his 89th birthday

headline: 'Adolescence' star Ashley Walters opens up about life after prison
subheadline: Ashley Walters' 'Animol' was released in UK cinemas on October 30, 2026
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Adolescence star Ashley Walters has a very personal reason for making his new film, Animol.

The actor is making his first film as a director and the story takes him back to a time in his own life that he has spoken openly about.

Ashley was just 19 when he was sent to a young offenders institute for having a gun. He spent 18 months in prison and life outside was not easy when he came home.

He stayed inside his house for three months because he did not feel ready to face people. The star, however, later said that everyone else's life had moved on, while he felt he had fallen behind.

READ MORE: 'Adolescence' star reveals how filming the series changed him

Ashley also started drinking to deal with what he was going through. His drinking became worse over the years and he found it hard to stop.

It took him 15 years to finally give up alcohol in 2020 as his wife, Danielle Isaie, was there for him when he needed help.

Since then, Ashley has made a name for himself in shows like Top Boy and Adolescence. Now, he is bringing some of his own memories to the screen.

READ MORE: Diddy hit with another setback as old controversy returns

Animol follows 15 year old Troy as he tries to get through life in a young offenders institute. Ashley wants the film to show what prison life is really like.

Adolescence star Ashley Walters has a very personal reason for making his new film, Animol.

The actor is making his first film as a director and the story takes him back to a time in his own life that he has spoken openly about.

Ashley was just 19 when he was sent to a young offenders institute for having a gun. He spent 18 months in prison and life outside was not easy when he came home.

He stayed inside his house for three months because he did not feel ready to face people. The star, however, later said that everyone else's life had moved on, while he felt he had fallen behind.

Ashley also started drinking to deal with what he was going through. His drinking became worse over the years and he found it hard to stop.

It took him 15 years to finally give up alcohol in 2020 as his wife, Danielle Isaie, was there for him when he needed help.

Since then, Ashley has made a name for himself in shows like Top Boy and Adolescence. Now, he is bringing some of his own memories to the screen.

headline: Suki Waterhouse addresses rumours she secretly married Robert Pattinson
subheadline: The 'Twilight' actor recently sparked rumours he secretly married the singer, much like Zendaya and Tom Holland
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson aren’t secretly married, after all.

In a new interview with The Sunday Times Style Magazine via Daily Mail, the singer opened up about her wedding plans with the Twilight star, with whom she shares a two-year-old daughter.

“It would either be all or nothing,” she said. “If we were going to go for it we'd have a massive party, blow it out.”

READ MORE: Did Robert Pattinson just confirm secret wedding to Suki Waterhouse?

Waterhouse, 34, and Pattinson, 40, have been together since 2018 and engaged for nearly three years. Earlier this year in February, Pattinson sparked rumours that secretly got married much like his The Drama costar Zendaya.

In June, In Touch Weekly reported that they're a “married couple.”

But according to Waterhouse’s latest comments, the couple haven’t even got around to wedding planning yet as they focus on their careers.

She admitted, “It's quite hard to make something work where you're both doing these kinds of jobs, when you don't live in one place and you're travelling a lot.”

Despite the challenges, she described their nearly decade-long relationship as “a beautiful thing,” adding that she feels “so happy” with the life they have built together.

The couple also hope to spend more time in West London next year, where they have applied for a primary school for their daughter.

READ MORE: Suki Waterhouse celebrates her daughter's 2nd birthday
